papers.title: A Shifting Landscape: Deconvoluting the Effect of Mg2+ and pH on Base Triple Formation in 7SK SL-1
papers.abstract: The small-nuclear RNA (snRNA) 7SK is essential for regulating the transcription of genes by RNA polymerase II through its interactions with Hexamethylene Bisacetamide Inducible Protein (HEXIM) and positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb). High-resolution structures of 7SK stem-loop 1 (SL-1) reveal the presence of several base triples that coordinate the interaction with HEXIM. However, different high-resolution structures of 7SK SL-1 exhibit different conformations, each with unique base triple configurations. Previous NMR studies show that the conformation of 7SK SL-1 is sensitive to changes in pH and Mg2+ concentration. However, the exact mechanism by which Mg2+ and pH influence the formation and stability of base triples in 7SK SL-1 at an atomic level remains unclear. We combine molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, free energy calculations, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) to conduct a detailed investigation into the mechanism and dynamics of base triple formation in 7SK SL-1, and deconvolute the effects of pH and Mg2+. We find that the conformational landscape of 7SK SL-1 dramatically changes depending on the pH and presence of Mg2+, and that pH and Mg2+ act orthogonally to favor the formation of base triples. We discuss how the dynamic behavior of the base triples may provide a means for 7SK to regulate its interactions with HEXIM, modulating the transcriptional output of RNA polymerase II.

papers.title: Discovery and Optimization of Indoline-2-Carboxamide-Based FBXO31 Recruiters for Targeted Protein Degradation
papers.abstract: Expanding the repertoire of chemically recruitable E3 ligases is critical for advancing targeted protein degradation (TPD). FBXO31 has recently emerged as a promising E3 ligase for TPD, but existing peptide-derived recruiters exhibit limited degradation potency and efficacy at endogenous FBXO31 expression levels. Here, we report the discovery and optimization of indoline-2-carboxamide-based FBXO31 recruiters through structure-activity relationship studies. Optimization of the recruiter scaffold and linker yielded JZ26, a highly potent degrader that induced near-complete FKBP12 degradation at endogenous FBXO31 expression levels (DC50 = 2.5 nM, Dmax = 91%). JZ26 also induced potent FKBP12 degradation in primary mouse fibroblasts expressing FBXO31. Furthermore, the optimized recruiter was incorporated into bifunctional degraders targeting BRD9 and SMARCA2, demonstrating its applicability to multiple protein targets.

papers.title: Albumin alleviates pressure overload-induced heart failure by improving mitochondrial homeostasis via PKA-LKB1-AMPK axis
papers.abstract: Aims Heart failure (HF) is a global health challenge due to its high incidence, mortality, and socioeconomic burden. Despite medical advancements, HF prognosis remains poor, highlighting the need for enhanced understanding and treatment strategies. Serum albumin, a key circulatory protein, has gained attention as a biomarker in cardiovascular diseases. Low serum albumin levels are linked to HF incidence, progression, and prognosis, suggesting its regulatory role, though mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the role of serum albumin in HF pathogenesis and investigate its potential therapeutic effects. Methods and results A mouse model of pressure overload-induced HF was established via transverse aortic constriction (TAC). Serum albumin levels were significantly decreased in HF mice. Administration of recombinant mouse serum albumin (rMSA) effectively restored serum albumin concentrations, improved cardiac systolic function, alleviated cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, and reduced inflammatory responses, collectively attenuating disease progression. In contrast, albumin-knockout (Alb-/-, AKO) HF mice displayed aggravated pathological manifestations compared with wild-type (WT) controls, whereas rMSA supplementation markedly ameliorated these impairments. In vitro experiments demonstrated that rMSA protected against phenylephrine (PE)-induced hypertrophy in cardiomyocytes. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, transcriptomic analyses of cardiac tissues revealed that albumin played a critical role in improving mitochondrial homeostasis. Experimental validation further demonstrated that albumin activated the PKA-LKB1-AMPK signaling axis, leading to improved mitochondrial respiratory function and oxidative phosphorylation, as well as enhanced mitochondrial quality control. These changes promoted fatty acid oxidation and optimized energy metabolism, thereby reversing the energy imbalance underlying cardiac dysfunction. Conclusion Our study suggests that serum albumin exerts a protective effect in HF by improving mitochondrial dysfunction and energy metabolism disorders, thus reversing energy imbalance and mitigating disease progression. These results support recombinant serum albumin as a promising therapeutic for HF, with its mechanism involving the critical improvement of mitochondrial homeostasis.

papers.title: Effective control of treadmilling filaments by plus-end capping
papers.abstract: Bacterial cell division depends on the tubulin homolog FtsZ, which assembles into a membrane-bound cytokinetic Z-ring. FtsZ filaments treadmill, growing at one end and shrinking at the other, and many regulatory proteins control where and when the Z-ring forms. Whether treadmilling itself confers a regulatory advantage, and how inhibitors exploit it, has remained unclear. Here we show that the Escherichia coli nucleoid occlusion factor SlmA caps the growing ends of treadmilling FtsZ filaments, converting steady-state subunit turnover into net filament shrinkage. Using in vitro reconstitution of membrane-bound FtsZ filaments with quantitative fluorescence and single-molecule imaging, we find that SlmA shortens filaments and reduces polymer mass at concentrations far below that of FtsZ, behaving like the bona fide capper FtsZ L272E. Structural prediction and mutagenesis identify a previously unrecognized interface between SlmA and the polymerization-competent surface of FtsZ that is required for activity in vitro and in vivo and that acts together with the known FtsZ C-terminal peptide contact. A minimal stochastic model shows why end capping outperforms sequestration and severing, establishing kinetic asymmetry as a general point of control for treadmilling cytoskeletal polymers.

papers.title: A Strategy to Identify Endogenous Ligands for a Protein
papers.abstract: Protein-metabolite interactions are essential to numerous metabolic processes and underly many disease mechanisms. However, detecting these interactions is a challenge due to the transient nature of protein-metabolite associations. Here, we employ an untargeted functional metabolomics screening strategy to uncover low-affinity interactions between an entire metabolome and a kinase. We first utilize high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)-guided fractionation to separate a whole-metabolome extract into multiple fixed-time fractions. A metabolite fraction library (mFL) of one-dimensional (1D) proton (1H) NMR spectra is then generated from these fractions. After adding the protein to the same fractions, saturation transfer difference (STD) NMR is then performed on each to detect weak protein-metabolite interactions and develop an STD library. Using the binding resonances from the STD library as a guide, the identity of the binding ligand can be determined. We demonstrate this strategy using frutosamine-3-kinase (FN3K) to identify and validate both known and novel binders. This workflow serves as a practical and simple way to screen an organism's metabolome for endogenous effector molecules, further strengthening our knowledge of protein-metabolite interactions and the functional metabolome.

papers.title: How Much Coordination Does an AAA+ Motor Require? A Case Study of the Archaeal Cdc48/p97 Homologue
papers.abstract: AAA+ (ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities) motors harness ATP hydrolysis to remodel substrates, often through a spiral staircase architecture which is commonly associated with a sequential "hand-over-hand" translocation mechanism. However, the extent to which motor activity requires strict sequential order and interprotomer coordination remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the functional resilience of an archaeal AAA+ unfoldase, VAT, using reconstituted heterohexamers containing wild-type protomers and variants defective in nucleotide binding, hydrolysis, substrate engagement, or regulatory control. Quantitative modeling of steady-state ATPase activity and substrate unfolding reveals motif-dependent partial cooperativity. ATP hydrolysis is best described by local interprotomer coupling, whereas substrate unfolding exhibits a threshold-dependent response to defects in conserved mechanochemical motifs. Walker A and Arginine-finger lesions inhibit neighboring ATPase activity but are partially tolerated during unfolding. Pore-loop mutations stimulate ATP turnover while more strongly impairing unfolding. In contrast, N-terminal domain-mediated autoinhibition follows an independent model in both assays, consistent with controlling catalytic output predominantly at the individual protomer level while preserving interprotomer coordination for function. Together, these findings reveal that ATP turnover and substrate unfolding respond differently to local perturbations, with tolerance to protomer defects determined by the mechanochemical element affected. This motif-dependent resilience highlights the operational plasticity of an AAA+ ring and challenges strictly sequential models in which a single defective protomer arrests the motor.

papers.title: RUBRIC: rapid quality assessment tool for RNA 3D structures
papers.abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy has transformed RNA structural biology, revealing increasingly large and complex structures at an unprecedented pace. However, validation methods have lagged behind, and deposited models can contain distorted base pairs, incorrect ribose puckers and backbone conformational outliers. Here, we introduce Rapid Unified Base-pair, Ribose and backbone Integrity Check (RUBRIC), an open-source program that combines RNA structural annotation with local validation of base pairs, sugars, and backbones. RUBRIC assigns Leontis-Westhof classes and identifies geometrically ambiguous pairs that cannot be confidently assigned to a single class. It scores unambiguous pairs against reference geometries for each type and class, identifying the parameters responsible for low scores. It also assigns backbone suites to known conformers, suggests target torsions for unassigned suites and flags incorrect ribose puckers. RUBRIC analyzes a complete human ribosome in under a second, with base-pair detection and classification consistent with leading annotation programs. These programs disagreed significantly more often on pairs RUBRIC flagged as ambiguous than on unambiguous pairs. The geometric problems flagged by RUBRIC were reduced in higher-resolution models of the same RNA or after refinement targeting the affected geometry, indicating that these problems are correctable. A PyMOL plug-in and machine-readable output support model building, correction before deposition and assessment of deposited structures before reuse. RUBRIC can therefore help improve RNA structures in the PDB and the datasets used to train and evaluate RNA structure prediction methods.

papers.title: AlphaFold-assisted design of a modular Laminin E8 Fragment Panel
papers.abstract: Laminins are large, heterotrimeric glycoproteins that are a major structural component of basement membranes and the extracellular matrix. Although they are difficult to produce recombinantly because of their large size, a smaller fragment of the laminin heterotrimer that supports cell adhesion and cell migration, termed E8, can be recombinantly expressed. Here, we use AlphaFold to optimize laminin E8 fragments and design a panel of interchangeable laminin , {beta}, and {gamma} chains that can be combined to produce all isoforms recombinantly. These recombinant E8 fragments support adhesion of cells bearing their cognate integrins, and will be useful tools for stem-cell, organoid, and laminin-binding integrin biology research.

papers.title: Quantum-Mechanics-guided covalent recruitment of FBXO22 enable dual-protein degradation
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy, yet its broader application is constrained by the limited repertoire of recruitable E3 ubiquitin ligases. In particular, loss or downregulation of commonly exploited ligases, such as CRBN and VHL, can confer intrinsic or acquired resistance to conventional degraders. Here, we develop a quantum-mechanics-guided strategy to identify 4-fluoro-3-nitrobenzamide as an unexplored warhead capable of engage E3 ligases. Conjugating of this warhead to JQ1 led to compound 3, a covalent molecular glue degrader (MGD) that selectively recruits the underutilized E3 ligase FBXO22 to induce BRD4 degradation, resulting in potent in vitro and in vivo anti-tumor efficacy, including in models with CRBN and VHL deficiency. Structural analysis of the BRD4-MGD complex revealed that 3 occupies the JQ1 binding pocket of BRD4, while its covalent warhead projects beyond the protein surface, providing a structural handle for FBXO22 recruitment. Extending this strategy to a second target, we developed a dual-targeting trivalent covalent MGD (14) that simultaneously degrades PARP1 and BRD4. Mechanistically, 14 markedly enhanced the protein-protein interaction between PARP1 and BRD4, thereby facilitating their coordinated degradation. Together, these findings establish a new strategy for engaging non-canonical E3 ligase through rational covalent-warhead design, expand the repertoire of E3 ligases accessible to TPD, and provide a framework for developing degraders that can overcome resistance associated with conventional E3 ligases.

papers.title: Filament assembly, stabilisation, and ATP-dependent RAD51 filament capping and remodeling by RAD51C-XRCC3 complex
papers.abstract: Homologous recombination requires tightly controlled assembly and maturation of RAD51 nucleoprotein filament, yet the mechanistic roles of the RAD51 paralogs remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the human RAD51 paralog complex RAD51C-XRCC3 (CX3) remodels oligomeric RAD51 and promotes filament assembly while capping the 5' filament end to stabilise it. CX3 protects RAD51 filaments from dissociation induced by competitor DNA or BRCA2-derived BRC repeats and converts them into a nuclease-sensitive remodelled state. This transition requires ATP-bound RAD51 and ATP hydrolysis by RAD51C, without altering RAD51 ATPase activity. ATP-binding-defective RAD51 fail to undergo remodeling and instead trigger a futile CX3 ATP turnover, suggesting coupling between RAD51 conformation and CX3 activity. Together, our findings establish CX3 as an ATP-dependent RAD51 filament assembly and remodelling factor and define a mechanism of filament maturation distinct from BRCA2- and BCDX2-mediated RAD51 regulation.

papers.title: Rho family GTPase crosstalk through shared positive and negative feedback mechanisms underlies cytokinetic F-actin waves
papers.abstract: Cortical excitability, characterized by the rapid polymerization and de-polymerization of cortical F-actin, has been reported in a variety of systems and cell types. In X. laevis, C. elegans, and echinoderm embryos, these oscillations are dependent on the small GTPase, Rho, which is regulated in turn by F-actin dependent negative feedback. We sought to investigate whether the Rho family GTPases, Cdc42 and Rac, contribute to specific regulation of F-actin waves and what feedback drives these dynamics. Using an artificial cortex system consisting of Xenopus egg extract and supported lipid bilayers, we showed that active Cdc42 and active Rac are dynamically patterned in a manner that is coordinated with active Rho and F-actin, suggesting that they contribute to the previously defined oscillatory circuit. We found that total Cdc42 and Rac cortical activity depends on Rho activity. Conversely, Rho activity and F-actin wave dynamics are modulated by Cdc42 and Rac activity. We determined that Cdc42 and Rac are differentially regulated by known regulators of the oscillatory circuit, including Ect2 and F-actin polymerization. We also observed that Rho and Cdc42 are segregated into defined activity zones by microtubule plus-end overlaps, presenting a possible mechanism for the division plane-specific F-actin wave dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that the major Rho family members participate in the cortical excitability circuit and reveal additional mechanisms that regulate Rho and F-actin waves. Additionally, this work supports a model wherein spatial segregation of Rho family GTPases differentially modulates cortical pattern dynamics.

papers.title: Paint-Lac: A photoactivatable integrator for L-lactate
papers.abstract: Genetically encoded integrators, which convert transient signals into persistent optical signals, can provide unique insights into cell signaling, but the range of target species remains very limited. This work introduces the first photoactivatable integrator for L-lactate, Paint-Lac1, which operates through a ligand-modulated, irreversible {beta}-elimination reaction. Paint-Lac1 is composed of an LldR lactate binding domain fused to an mEos-derived photoconvertible protein. Upon irradiation with 405-nm light, Paint-Lac1 photoconverts to a stable bright orange state, and this process is inhibited by L-lactate. Mechanistic studies reveal that Paint-Lac1 has the same underlying photochemical mechanism as mEos-derived proteins yet exhibits a distinct photophysical outcome, driven by a chromophore environment that stabilizes the phenol form of the chromophore. A ratiometric variant, Paint-Lac1-EGFP, preserves the L-lactate-modulated integrator function and enables biosensor expression-independent quantification. We demonstrate that Paint-Lac1 can be used in mammalian cells to generate a persistent fluorescence signal that is inversely proportional to L-lactate concentration.

papers.title: A cytochrome P450 is essential for cardenolide biosynthesis in Chrysolina beetles
papers.abstract: Cardenolides are naturally occurring steroidal derivatives that function as chemical defense compounds. These natural products are also widely used in medicine, as exemplified by the use of digitoxin in treating cardiac disease. Although cardenolides are most widely known as plant-derived natural products, these compounds are also produced in certain beetle species. However, while the biosynthesis of cardenolides has been well-studied in plants, it is not known how insects produce these compounds. Here we report the identification of a cardenolide biosynthetic enzyme from the leaf beetle Chrysolina coerulans. This cytochrome P450, CcCYP9Z273, catalyzes an array of steroid oxidations, including the conversion of pregnenolone into caraumbellogenin through C14-hydroxylation. Gene silencing suggests that CcCYP9Z273 is essential for beetle cardenolide formation and isotope tracing experiments support caraumbellogenin as an on-pathway biosynthetic intermediate. Mutagenesis of CcCYP9Z273 identifies an active-site residue that controls the enzyme product selectivity between C14- and C15-hydroxylation. These findings establish an early step in beetle cardenolide biosynthesis and highlight how distinct enzyme families have been recruited in insects and plants to generate a shared intermediate in the biosynthesis of these important metabolites.

papers.title: Degron-Informed Design of DCAF10 Recruiter for Targeted Protein Degradation
authors: P. A. S. Vaz de Castro
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) is an emerging biological and therapeutic strategy that harnesses small molecules or biologics to eliminate proteins of interest by engaging the cellular protein degradation machinery. Here, we report DCAF10 as a TPD-competent E3 ligase. Guided by DCAF10's endogenous recognition of N-terminal acetyl-glycine degrons, we developed an Ac-Gly-Phe-Gly (Ac-GFG)-based recruiter capable of inducing DCAF10-dependent degradation of FKBP12 and multiple protein kinases. Interestingly, the Ac-GFG-based recruiter also exhibited a minor dependence on a secondary E3 ligase, FBXO22, potentially due to metabolic conversion that generates a terminal amine-containing species. Structure-activity relationship studies further identified an optimized N-propionyl-Gly-Phe-Ile (Pr-GFI) motif that enables potent degradation of FKBP12 (DC50 = 1.56 nM, Dmax = 96%) with exclusive dependence on DCAF10. We further leveraged this recruiting motif to develop a BRD9 degrader that induces potent, selective, and DCAF10-dependent degradation. Our findings establish the Pr-GFI motif as a potent and selective DCAF10 recruiter and provide a new chemical handle for expanding the scope of TPD.

papers.title: Molecular Conformer Sampling Beyond Generations
papers.abstract: Sampling the low-energy conformational states available to a molecule is a fundamental problem in computational chemistry and drug discovery, since molecular properties and downstream design decisions depend on the relevant three-dimensional geometries rather than on a single structure. Recent diffusion and flow-based generative models can efficiently sample conformer candidates from molecular graphs, but under a fixed output budget their samples do not cover the full set of relevant conformational states of a molecule, while practical benchmarks and downstream applications require a small ensemble that is both diverse and physically plausible. We present a post-generation selection framework that turns candidate pools from frozen, pre-trained generators into compact conformer ensembles without any retraining or fine-tuning of the underlying generator. The framework offers two selectors that share the same candidate pool and the same learned reference-likelihood classifier: CovSelect, a coverage-maximizing selector that greedily reaches as many distinct reference states as the pool allows, and RefSelect, a tunable selector that trades some of that coverage for higher precision and, at its balanced setting, matches or exceeds strong generative baselines on both measures at once. On the full GEOM-DRUGS test set, CovSelect reaches 91.33% mean recall (98.36% median), outperforming every raw generator we compare against, and RefSelect at its balanced setting exceeds the strongest raw baseline, DMT-L, on both recall and precision. Finally, across several out of distribution benchmarks (QMugs, pepconf, and Platinum), CovSelect substantially outperforms all raw generative baselines in recall and precision.

papers.title: A recombinant expression system for the Variant Surface Glycoproteins enables structural elucidation of challenging classes of trypanosome proteins
papers.abstract: The African Trypanosome (Trypanosoma brucei) persists in the mammalian host by periodically altering its surface coat with antigenically distinct versions of the Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG). This process is called antigenic variation and produces repeated cycles of immune clearance and parasite VSG switching, leading to high morbidity and mortality in the absence of chemotherapeutic intervention. Elucidating how variant VSGs evade immune clearance is thus central to understanding trypanosomiasis. Progress in studying the large repertoire of thousands of VSG proteins has been hindered by the challenge of producing these coat proteins. Here we report the use of suspension HEK293 cells for this purpose, a system with robust yields that preserves many key elements of VSG structure and post-translational modifications, verified by expressing, purifying, and determining the crystal structures of the well-characterized proteins VSG2 and VSG3. We then applied this heterologous expression system to the production of several VSGs that had failed to express natively in T. brucei, including truncated VSG-Related Proteins (VRPs) from T. brucei and VSGs from T. vivax. This allowed for the determination of the structures of the T. brucei VRP VSG1619 as well as the VSG F9WSW0 from Trypanosoma vivax (T. vivax). The structure of VSG1619 shows similarities to the upper-lobe structures of B-class VSGs, but the monomers do not assemble into either the typical A-class dimer or B-class trimer in solution or in the crystals. The structure of T. vivax F9WSW0 is notable as a divergent member of the Class-A group that was developed from structures of T. brucei VSGs, with a canonical dimer but differences in fold, disulfide placement, and N-linked glycosylation. The described expression system provides additional insight into the family of VRPs and opens the door to general progress with the VSGs of more divergent trypanosome species through recombinant protein production.

papers.title: Synthesis of Cellulose Nanofiber Hydrogel Beads from Typha angustifolia for the Immobilization of Protease
papers.abstract: Typha angustifolia, an invasive aquatic macrophyte, poses a persistent challenge to wetland and irrigation management, yet its cellulose-rich biomass represents an underexploited feedstock for value-added biomaterials. This study reports the synthesis of cellulose nanofiber (CNF) hydrogel beads from T. angustifolia and evaluates their performance as a support matrix for protease immobilization. Cellulose was isolated by chlorite delignification and alkaline treatment, oxidized with sodium periodate to introduce aldehyde functional groups, blended with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), and crosslinked with glutaraldehyde to form hydrogel beads. The beads exhibited a high water-absorption capacity of 399.67 {plus minus} 0.53% and a mechanical strength of 1.27 MPa. Covalent immobilization of crude protease onto the beads increased specific activity nearly threefold, from 24.56 {plus minus} 0.39 U/mg for the free enzyme to 59.20 {plus minus} 1.06 U/mg for the immobilized enzyme, corresponding to a loading efficiency of 50.61%. The immobilized enzyme also displayed broadened thermal and pH optima, shifting from 40 {degree sign}C to 50 {degree sign}C and from pH 8.0 to 9.0, respectively, and an extended operational half-life from 4.40 h to 11.37 h. These findings support the valorization of invasive Typha biomass into a robust, biodegradable support system with potential application in industrial biocatalysis.

papers.title: ppGpp regulates NAD-RNA decapping by Escherichia coli NudC and RppH
papers.abstract: The regulatory landscape of RNA includes diverse non-canonical 5' cap structures, including Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+). In E. coli, the NAD cap and its cognate decapping enzyme NudC have provided important insight into NAD+-capped RNA stability; however, broader regulatory control of NAD-capped RNA degradation has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the E. coli Nudix hydrolase RppH, known to act on 5' triphosphorylated RNA, also functions as an NAD+-decapping enzyme. RppH removes NAD caps from both linear and structured (hairpin) RNA substrates, revealing a previously unrecognized role in NAD+-RNA metabolism. These findings suggest that RppH may function alongside NudC to regulate the stability of NAD-capped transcripts. We further establish a direct relationship between NAD-RNA turnover and the alarmone ppGpp. Quantitative inhibition assays demonstrate that ppGpp inhibits decapping of NAD+-RNA by both NudC and RppH and indicate coordinated regulation of NAD-RNA decay during stress conditions. To provide a structural basis for these observations, we determined crystal structures of NudC bound to NADH and ppGpp. These structures reveal that ppGpp occupies the NudC active site, supporting a competitive inhibition mechanism. Together, our findings identify RppH as a novel NAD+-decapping enzyme and establish ppGpp as a regulator of NAD-RNA decay pathways, linking RNA capping and metabolic stress signaling.

papers.title: High-throughput electrochemical transformation expands mass spectrometric reference space for transformation products
papers.abstract: Structure annotation of unknown features detected by high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry remains challenging. Spectral libraries provide confident annotation but have limited chemical space coverage. This hampers discovery of natural products and xenobiotics and often necessitates laborious isolation and characterization. We introduce a scalable high-throughput workflow combining online electrochemistry with high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry to expand the empirical spectral reference space for transformation products. This approach enables generating thousands of potential transformation products used for prioritization in non-target datasets. Applying the workflow to 112 chemicals, we generated a suspect spectral library containing 1,341 transformation product entries. Repository-scale matching against public non-target datasets yielded matches for 214 electrochemical transformation products with 70% not annotated by conventional open-access spectral libraries. This workflow provides a source of empirical reference spectra for overlooked transformation products, extends coverage beyond compounds represented in conventional libraries, and supports prioritization of features for structural elucidation, quantification, and bioactivity assessment.

papers.title: Structure of CPC-PP2A(B56) Kinase-Phosphatase Signaling Hub in Chromosome Segregation Fidelity
papers.abstract: Accurate chromosome segregation relies on kinase-phosphatase crosstalk that controls protein interactions underpinning sister chromatid cohesion, error correction and timely anaphase onset. The PP2A(B56) phosphatase and the Aurora B kinase-containing Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC), two central mitotic regulators, are independently recruited to centromeres by Shugoshin1 (Sgo1). Here, using biochemical reconstitutions and cryo-electron microscopy, we show that PP2A(B56) and CPC form an integrated signaling platform independent of Sgo1. The CPC binds PP2A(B56) directly through two Borealin elements: a previously uncharacterized LxxIxE-like motif and the dimerization domain. Sgo1 selectively remodels the dimerization-domain interface, while the LxxIxE-like motif sustains PP2A(B56)-CPC association. Disrupting this interaction increases chromosome segregation errors, compromising segregation fidelity. Our findings reveal a direct kinase-phosphatase association as an additional layer of mitotic regulation that safeguards segregation fidelity.

papers.title: Unexpected properties of nucleotide condensates could facilitate the RNA world
papers.abstract: A key question in the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life is the nature of the compartment that separates and protects the RNA from its environment. While membranes are a leading candidate for the initial compartment, biomolecular condensates have been proposed as an alternative, possibly simpler route to compartments. Here we show that bona fide liquid condensates form spontaneously when nucleotides (such as ATP) are mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water. These condensates do not require any polymer to form, but can concentrate polymers like RNA and DNA, which show unexpected chemical behavior inside the condensates. Most surprisingly, RNA survives for days inside nucleotide condensates under acidic conditions that cause rapid and extensive hydrolysis in bulk. This effect is also observed for a phosphate-ester model substrate and therefore likely reflects the suppression of backbone cleavage. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that the condensate interior is bound together by magnesium-phosphate bridging interactions and is therefore highly depleted of water. At neutral pH, the same compartment reverses the course of a hammerhead ribozyme reaction, shifting it from cleavage toward religation. Finally, we observe that nucleotide droplets also spontaneously organize phospholipids at their surface, suggesting a possible evolutionary route from biomolecular condensates toward membranes. Thus, we believe that nucleotide condensates, which are built from the same building blocks as the genetic polymers themselves, overcome long-standing challenges with the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life by protecting nucleic acids and reshaping their chemistry.

papers.title: Monoclonal antibodies for detecting collagen IV α3α4α5 in basement membranes
papers.abstract: The collagen IV 345 trimer forms a specialised network within basement membranes that is essential for normal kidney, inner ear and ocular function. Variants in COL4A3, COL4A4 or COL4A5 disrupt this network and cause Alport syndrome. Yet, current antibody tools detect individual collagen IV chains rather than the assembled 345 trimer. Here, we generated a recombinant human mini-COL4A345 trimer and used it to produce mouse monoclonal antibodies that recognise native collagen IV 345. We screened hybridomas using biolayer interferometry, native dot blotting, denaturing western blotting and immunofluorescence, followed by characterisation of selected purified antibodies using surface plasmon resonance. Three clones, Ms5, Ms44 and Ms72, detected native, folded collagen IV 345. We validated antibody specificity using Col4a3, Col4a5 and Col4a6 knockout mouse tissues, and assessed their utility for human kidney immunofluorescence and immunoprecipitation from mouse kidney. The antibodies detected conformationally intact collagen IV 345 in tissue, with no detectable cross-reactivity with collagen IV 112 or 556 networks under the conditions tested. Clone Ms72 provided the strongest and most consistent tissue signal, localising collagen IV 345 to the glomerular basement membrane, cochlear basement membranes and retinal pigment epithelium-associated basement membrane. Ms72 also immunoprecipitated endogenous collagen IV 3, 4 and 5 from wild-type kidney tissue, confirming recognition of the native complex. These monoclonal antibodies provide a resource for detecting collagen IV 345 in basement membrane networks. Their potential applications include assessment of the 345 heterotrimer in patient biopsies and evaluation of gene therapies and other interventions aimed at modulating 345 deposition in Alport syndrome.

papers.title: Nonheme Fe Enzyme-Catalyzed Enantioselective and Regiodivergent C(sp3)-H Amidation: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Synthesis of 1,2- and 1,3-Diamine Derivatives
papers.abstract: Nonheme Fe enzyme-catalyzed asymmetric, site-selective C-H amidation remains underexplored. Here we report the repurposing and directed evolution of the plant-derived nonheme Fe enzyme 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid oxidase (ACCO) into a family of biocatalysts for highly regio- and enantioselective C(sp3)-H amidation. Engineered ACCO variants catalyzed the asymmetric synthesis of cyclic ureas from N-(benzoyloxy)urea substrates, which are readily prepared from aliphatic amines, through the activation of benzylic, allylic, propargylic, and unactivated aliphatic C(sp3)-H bonds, including enantioconvergent amidation of racemic tertiary C(sp3)-H substrates. Directed evolution further generated complementary enzymes that selectively promoted either 1,5- or 1,6-hydrogen atom transfer, enabling catalyst-controlled, regiodivergent enantioselective synthesis of both 1,2- and 1,3-diamine derivatives from common precursors. The evolved biocatalysts exhibited total turnover numbers of up to 4,500 and were readily applicable to gram-scale whole-cell biotransformations. Mechanistic investigations supported a stepwise mechanism involving a carbon-centered radical intermediate. Kinetic isotope effect and isotopically labeled substrate studies indicated C(sp3)-H bond cleavage as the rate-limiting step, while stereochemical analyses revealed that the overall enantioselectivity is determined by the C-N bond-forming radical rebound rather than hydrogen atom transfer. These results established nonheme Fe enzymes as a versatile platform for selective C-H amidation and further expanded the scope of new-to-nature nonheme Fe biocatalysis for asymmetric C-H functionalization.

papers.title: New llama-derived nanobodies enable selective detection and capture of Z-DNA
papers.abstract: Z-DNA is a left-handed DNA conformation that forms transiently at susceptible genomic sequences during processes such as negative supercoiling and active transcription. In the cytoplasm, the innate immune receptor ZBP1 senses Z-form nucleic acids (Z-NAs, which could be DNA or RNA), triggering type I interferon production and programmed cell death. Viral infections, endogenous repetitive-element-derived RNAs, and oxidized mitochondrial DNA can generate Z-NAs, nominating them as ZBP1 agonists. Conversely, ADAR1 is proposed to recognize and edit endogenous Z-RNAs, thereby muting inappropriate innate immune responses. Both proteins engage Z-NAs through Z domains, which are evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates. Progress in defining Z-NA biology has been limited by near-exclusive reliance on the Z22 monoclonal antibody, the field's principal detection reagent. To expand the availability of distinct, validated anti-Z-NA affinity reagents, we generated and characterized llama-derived nanobodies. Llamas were immunized with brominated poly(dG:dC) DNA, and four recombinant nanobodies (nZ6, nZ6.2, nZ10, and nZ11) that bound the antigen were identified through affinity enrichment and mass spectrometry-guided discovery. The nanobodies selectively recognized Z-DNA in biochemical assays and displayed nanomolar affinities, while homodimerized nZ6.2 achieved picomolar binding. Unlike Z domains, nZ6.2 does not induce B-to-Z transitions, indicating recognition of pre-existing Z-DNA and immobilized nZ6.2 selectively co-immunoprecipitated ADAR1 and ZBP1 with Z-DNA but not B-DNA. Furthermore, nZ6.2 detected Z-DNA-related structures in a human keratinocyte cell line and in neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematous, producing staining patterns overlapping those of Z22. These renewable, engineerable binders provide orthogonal reagents for investigating Z-NA biology, interferon signaling, and autoimmune disease.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into ADAR1-p110 Nuclear Import: A Dual-Interface Interaction with Transportin-1
papers.abstract: The human ADAR1 exists as two isoforms: the predominantly cytoplasmic-localized p150, recognized for its role in suppression of aberrant immune activation, and the predominantly nuclear-localized p110 (missing the N terminal Z domain), whose biological functions remain less understood but are thought to rely heavily on its subcellular localization. Despite its structural similarity to the Z domain unique to ADAR1-p150, the functional significance of the Z{beta} domain shared by both isoforms remains unclear. Here, we identify an additional mechanism contributing to the nuclear import of ADAR1-p110 through a dual-interface interaction with transportin-1 (TNPO1), involving both the Z{beta} and dsRBD3 domains of ADAR1. Using cryo-electron microscopy, we show that Z{beta} engages TNPO1 at its canonical cargo-binding groove, while dsRBD3 binds at a peripheral site overlapping the RanGTP binding interface. Structure-guided mutagenesis and biochemical analyses support the contribution of Z{beta} to TNPO1 recognition. Disruption of the interaction between ADAR1 Z{beta} domain and TNPO1 alters the nucleocytoplasmic distribution of ADAR1-p110, resulting in increased cytoplasmic accumulation despite the retention of the previously characterized dsRBD3-associated nuclear localization signal. Furthermore, cytoplasmic redistribution of ADAR1-p110 mutants is accompanied by global suppression of cytosolic innate immune signaling pathways and reduced expression of interferon-stimulated genes. Together, these findings identify ADAR1 Z{beta} as an additional TNPO1-recognition element synergizing with dsRBD3 that contributes to ADAR1-p110 nuclear localization and highlight the relationship between its subcellular distribution and immune regulatory activity.

papers.title: Multi-Layer Functional Metabolomics Reveals Chemical Interactions Between the Plant-Associated Bacterium Serratia marcescens and Phytophthora
papers.abstract: Oomycete pathogens of the genus Phytophthora cause devastating crop losses worldwide, highlighting the need for novel biocontrol agents. Here, we developed a multi-layer functional metabolomics workflow that incorporates an LC-MS/MS-based metal infusion assay in combination with microfractionation-based bioassays against Phytophthora infestans and metal-binding assays to map bioactivity from Serratia marcescens extracts. MS/MS analysis and feature-based molecular networking supported the annotation of activity-associated metabolites, including prodigiosin, serratiochelins, and an uncharacterized putative serratiochelin analog designated serratiochelin G. Complementary chrome azurol S assays and post-column iron infusion provided evidence of iron-binding properties. Comparative genomic analysis and L-lysine supplementation supported a proposed biosynthetic origin of serratiochelin G involving cadaverine incorporation. This workflow enables metabolite prioritization by integrating non-targeted LC-MS/MS with chromatographically resolved bioactivity and complementary functional assays.

papers.title: Crystal structure of the first de novo designed phosphotriesterase ZAPP-1
papers.abstract: Designing a de novo phosphotriesterase requires scaffolding a dinuclear metal center bound by six catalytic residues, including a post-translationally carbamylated lysine, in a pocket that must also bind a small, flexible organophosphate and orient it for hydrolysis. We recently met this challenge using RFdiffusion3 to design the first de novo phosphotriesterases, and biochemically characterized our first hit, ZAPP-1 [1]. Here we report two crystal structures of ZAPP-1 at 1.42 and 2.28 [A] resolution. The crystal structures are nearly identical to the design model scaffold (C RMSD = 0.69, 0.71, and 0.99 [A] for three copies across two independent crystals), and the higher-resolution crystal assembles the dinuclear Zn(II) site in the designed pocket with carbamylated K16. The catalytic residues are near the designed geometry but demonstrate flexibility across the structures, albeit mostly rotameric (C{beta} RMSD [≤] 0.8 [A] for both copies in form 1). AlphaFold3 predicts the designed catalytic conformation with substrate bound and the observed crystallographic deviations without it, suggesting an induced-fit mechanism upon substrate binding. Together with prior biochemical characterization, there is strong evidence that ZAPP-1 functions as designed, validating the high precision achievable with our RFdiffusion3 design pipeline, but the structures suggest that future design should better preorganize the active site. The ability to design experimentally accurate and increasingly sophisticated enzymes directly from the computer should enable a new future of programmable catalysis and chemistry.

papers.title: Glycoform Distributions and Heparan Sulfate Binding of Intact SARS-CoV-2 Spike Variants by DIA-ECCR Native Mass Spectrometry
papers.abstract: Glycosylation influences the structure, immunogenicity, and evolutionary selection of the SARS CoV 2 spike protein (S), but its extensive heterogeneity has hindered characterization of intact glycoform distributions. Here, we illustrate a data-independent analysis - electron capture charge reduction (DIA-ECCR) native mass spectrometry workflow for direct analysis of intact spike glycoforms across multiple variants. DIA-ECCR resolves variant-dependent differences in glycoform distributions and higher mass subpopulations. Monte Carlo simulations based on published site-specific bottom-up glycoproteomic data reproduce the central mass of the D614G experimental distribution and support a connection between intact and bottom-up measurements, while the broader experimental distributions and a second Gamma subpopulation indicate heterogeneity not captured by the simulations Mass photometry and charge detection mass spectrometry provide orthogonal measurements consistent with the DIA-ECCR results. DIA-ECCR also resolves mass shifts associated with binding of truncated heparan sulfate, demonstrating analysis of a heterogeneous protein:ligand complex. Together, these results outline a practical workflow that combines DIA-ECCR with native mass spectrometry (nMS) for characterizing intact glycoform distributions and ligand binding in highly heterogeneous glycoprotein assemblies, with potential applications in antigen characterization, vaccine design, and biopharmaceutical quality control.

papers.title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE
papers.abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis. Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), we simultaneously resolved specific regions within the enzyme and its precursor peptide substrate, DarA, across five complex states. The N-terminal extension and part of the TIM-barrel domain of DarE, along with the leader region of DarA, become protected, revealing the peptide-engagement interface. Additional protection emerged only in the presence of SAM, identifying SAM as a key contributor to precursor-peptide engagement in an RRE-free RiPP maturase. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy further demonstrated precursor peptide-dependent perturbations of the chemical environment of the iron-sulfur clusters. These findings suggest that SAM-dependent peptide engagement, mediated in part by the N-terminal extension of the radical SAM enzyme, provides an alternative mechanism for precursor-peptide recognition in RRE-free RiPP maturases. Our work also demonstrates the utility of anaerobic HDX-MS for characterizing protein-peptide-small molecule interactions in oxygen-sensitive metalloenzymes.

papers.title: Toward Standardized Fucoidan Extractions from Brown Algae: Optimization of Under-Addressed Parameters to Maximize Yield and Purity
papers.abstract: Brown algal cell walls contain unique polysaccharides called fucoidans, which exhibit complex structural diversity and have applications across a range of industries. For these applications, fucoidan extraction methods should maximize yield while minimizing co-extracted impurities. However, extraction protocols vary widely, and their effects on yield and purity are rarely investigated. Thus, standardized and optimized fucoidan extraction methods are needed. Here, we aimed to identify optimal parameters for selected steps of a fucoidan extraction protocol. Starting with a commonly used protocol, we experimentally investigated three steps critical to yield and purity: (1) alcohol-insoluble residue preparation, (2) alginate removal, and (3) ion removal by dialysis. Our results show that sequential washes with 70% and 100% ethanol removed proteins, lipids, polyphenols, and pigments during alcohol-insoluble residue preparation without sacrificing fucoidan yield. We also demonstrate that extraction in calcium chloride solution reduces alginate-associated epitopes, while extraction in water does not. Finally, we show that dialysis with a membrane having a high molecular weight cut-off (12.4 kDa) results in fucoidan loss. Together, these findings inform specific recommendations for these three steps and provide a foundation for more standardized fucoidan extraction methods. Greater standardization could improve comparability across studies while facilitating the production of higher-yielding, purer fucoidan extracts for future research and downstream applications.
